The barbel drum Ctenosciaena gracilicirrhus is a small sciaenid species found along the Atlantic coast of South America, where it inhabits shallow continental shelf waters. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a relatively modest maximum size, with the ultimate total length recorded at 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a dimension that is consistent with its position as one of the smaller members of the family Sciaenidae. Length-frequency distributions from trawl samples further reveal that the total length at puberty is approximately 10 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10 centimeters], marking the size at which half of the sampled individuals exhibit gonadal development. This early onset of reproductive size compared to the maximum length suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early maturation over continued somatic growth, a pattern commonly observed in small-bodied, short-lived marine teleosts inhabiting productive coastal environments. The growth trajectory implied by these two length benchmarks points toward a relatively compressed juvenile phase before individuals transition into the reproductively active segment of the population.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) quantifies the proportion of body mass made up of ovarian tissue in this sciaenid. For populations maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index was estimated at 3% [GSI = 3%]. The consistency of this index across related species suggests a conserved physiological constraint on reproductive tissue formation within the family, potentially linked to the energetic demands of sustaining metabolic activity in warm coastal waters.

The early life stages of Ctenosciaena gracilicirrhus begin with the production of pelagic eggs that are remarkably small, reflecting a high fecundity, low per-offspring investment strategy typical of many coastal sciaenids. Based on the average egg diameter of 0.6 millimeters observed in histological sections, the estimated wet weight at birth of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is approximately 0.0001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0001 grams], a minuscule mass that underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early larval stage. This tiny body size at eclosion places the newly emerged prolarva within the size spectrum of ichthyoplankton that relies on a brief period of endogenous nutrition from the yolk reserves before the onset of gape-limited exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of these limited yolk stores imposes a critical window for successful first feeding, and the timing local water temperature, particularly around 26.1 °C, as observed in laboratory rearing experiments, strongly influences the rate of yolk absorption and subsequent larval survival.

Growth through the juvenile stage culminates in the attainment of a maximum adult body size, and for this species the ultimate wet weight has been determined from length-weight regressions based on the length-at-puberty and asymptotic length relationships. The maximum recorded adult body mass for Ctenosciaena gracilicirrhus is estimated at 100.5 grams [Wwi = 100.5 grams], a value derived from the allometric equation W = 0.00851 multiplied by total length raised to the power of 3.08. In parallel, the wet weight at puberty for females, calculated using the same length-weight relationship applied to the length at puberty of 10 centimeters, is 10.2 grams [Wwp = 10.2 grams]. The substantial difference between the mass at puberty and the asymptotic mass indicates that females continue to add considerable somatic tissue after reaching reproductive maturity, investing energy into both body growth and egg production simultaneously over multiple spawning seasons, a hallmark of indeterminate growth characteristic of teleosts.

The lifespan of Ctenosciaena gracilicirrhus in its natural habitat has been inferred from otolith annulus counts and mark-recapture studies, revealing that individuals living at a sustained water temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] have a maximum documented longevity of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This relatively extended lifespan, when considered alongside the modest asymptotic body size, suggests a life-history strategy in which slow, steady growth continues over many years rather than a rapid approach to a large terminal size. Such a pattern is consistent with the environmental conditions of the species' subtropical range, where stable thermal regimes and reliable prey availability may reduce the metabolic costs of senescence. The interplay between this decadal lifespan and the early onset of reproduction at 10 centimeters in total length creates a reproductive window spanning the majority of the adult phase, allowing for numerous spawning events across an individual's lifetime despite the modest per-event gonadal investment indicated by the low gonado-somatic index.
